rule.description: An interactive driver function has absorbed the bodies of other functions: it either reproduces the distinctive statement shapes of a same-file worker function inside itself, or spells out by hand the shared stdin read idiom (flush, scanf into a variable, line drain) that the repository's input utilities already provide. The function is flagged as oversized by readability-function-size (line threshold 55), so the absorbed logic sits in one of the largest functions in the tree.

checks.description: A function flagged as oversized by the readability-function-size sensor contains the distinctive statement shapes of a still-defined same-file worker function (at least 3 unique non-trivial statement shapes, at least 60% of that helper's shapes), meaning the helper's body is duplicated inside the caller rather than called by it.
checks.detected_relation: oversized caller function -> body of a same-file worker function reproduced inside it
checks.why_this_is_the_smell: Deeply inlined methods grow by absorbing other functions' implementations. When a caller carries a same-file helper's body inside itself, the helper survives only as duplicated logic (dead or twice-maintained) and the caller's abstraction boundary has collapsed: the deep-inline repair is to extract the absorbed body back into a callable function at the right level.

checks.description: A function flagged as oversized by the readability-function-size sensor spells out, by hand, the repository's stdin read idiom (fflush, scanf into a variable address, then a getchar drain loop) at one or more prompt sites, instead of calling the shared input-utility routine that exists for exactly this purpose.
checks.detected_relation: oversized caller function -> shared input-utility read sequence duplicated inline at each prompt site
checks.why_this_is_the_smell: Deeply inlined methods absorb not just same-file helpers but shared utility routines. A hand-written flush/read/drain sequence inside an oversized function is the utility's implementation copied into the caller at every prompt; extracting it back into one callable read routine is the deep-inline repair at the correct level.
